questions.question: A student says 'doubling the concentration doubles the rate constant'. Untangle the error: what does each quantity depend on?
questions.solution: Rate depends on concentration (rate = k[A]^x) and temperature; the rate CONSTANT k depends only on temperature (and catalyst) — it is the rate at unit concentration. Doubling [A] changes the rate, not k. Confusing the two is the most common kinetics error in exams.

questions.concept: Order must be found, not read
questions.question: For the reaction 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, why can you NOT write rate = k[NO]²[O₂] just from the stoichiometry?
questions.solution: Stoichiometry gives MOLECULARITY only for an elementary step. Order is an experimental quantity — the exponents that fit the observed rate law. (For this reaction the observed law is rate = k[NO]²[O₂], but that must be MEASURED, e.g. by initial-rates, not assumed.) Molecularity is a mechanism concept; order is a kinetics fact.

questions.question: Why does a first-order reaction's half-life stay constant while a zero-order reaction's halves as it proceeds? Use both half-life expressions.
questions.solution: First order: t½ = 0.693/k — no concentration term, so every successive half-life is identical (a defining signature used to identify first order). Zero order: t½ = [A]₀/2k — proportional to the remaining concentration, so each half-life is half the previous. The concentration-dependence of t½ distinguishes the orders.

questions.question: Why does a 10 K temperature rise roughly double many reaction rates, when average molecular energy changes only slightly?
questions.solution: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT): the fraction of molecules with energy ≥ Ea is an EXPONENTIAL function of temperature. Even a small rise in T sharply multiplies the fraction clearing the activation barrier — the tail of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution grows much faster than the average. The exponential sensitivity, not the mean energy, is the mechanism.

questions.question: A catalyst speeds a reaction a million-fold. What does it change, what does it NOT change, and why can it not make a non-spontaneous reaction go?
questions.solution: A catalyst provides an alternative path with lower activation energy (for both forward and reverse directions equally). It does NOT change ΔG, E°cell, K, or the final equilibrium composition — only how FAST equilibrium is reached. Since spontaneity depends on ΔG, a catalyst cannot start a thermodynamically uphill reaction.

questions.question: State which straight-line plot identifies each of zero, first and second order, and what the slope gives.
questions.solution: Zero: [A] vs t linear, slope = −k. First: ln[A] vs t linear, slope = −k. Second: 1/[A] vs t linear, slope = +k. The test is plotting the same data all three ways and seeing which is straight — a common practical-exam and theory question.

questions.question: Hydrolysis of ethyl acetate by water is bimolecular, yet follows first-order kinetics. Explain the 'pseudo' label.
questions.solution: Rate = k[ester][H₂O], but water is the SOLVENT — its concentration (~55.5 M) is so vast that it barely changes during the reaction. [H₂O] is effectively constant and folds into k: rate = k′[ester], first-order behaviour from a bimolecular mechanism. Excess of one reagent makes its concentration part of the constant — that is the pseudo-first-order condition.

questions.question: Why do many gas reactions occur far less often than the collision frequency predicts, even when the molecules collide with E ≥ Ea?
questions.solution: Collision theory adds an ORIENTATION (steric) factor P: molecules must collide with the reactive ends aligned for bond reorganisation. Randomly oriented high-energy collisions bounce off unreacted. Rate = P·Z·e^(−Ea/RT) — the fraction meeting BOTH the energy and orientation conditions is far smaller than the energy condition alone.
